precepts.text: And after him rose up Nathan to prophesy in the time of David. So we know who this is speaking of.
precepts.point: You see how Satan can deceive you. Satan put that lust in him to where he just did not care, and he went the extra mile: later in the story he put Uriah in the front of the battle and got him killed, then took the wife. What he saw became desire, desire became action, he tried to cover it up, and the consequences came: the child died.
precepts.why:
“And after him rose up Nathan to prophesy in the time of David.” So we know who we are talking about: this is David, in the days of Nathan the prophet, the prophet the Lord sent to him after Bathsheba. The next verse carries on: “As is the fat taken away from the peace offering, so was David chosen out of the children of Israel.”

That is the same David of 2 Samuel 11. He went out on the roof, “he saw a woman washing herself; and the woman was very beautiful to look upon.” Bad to the bone. He sent and inquired: I got power, let me send some people over there, let me make this official. One with a spiritual mind made it plain: this is the wife of Uriah the Hittite, this is somebody's wife, bro. “And David sent messengers, and took her” anyway. Wisdom and understanding were right there, and he pushed them aside.

“and she came in unto him, and he lay with her”. She wasn't right either. She didn't resist, she wasn't opposed; she thought she came up. “And the woman conceived, and sent and told David, and said, I am with child.”

You see how Satan can deceive you. Satan put that lust in him to where he just didn't care, and he went the extra mile: he put Uriah in the front of the battle, got him killed, and took the wife. What he saw, the desire, the action, the cover-up, and the consequences: his first child was gone. Yet Sirach remembers David as the one chosen out of the children of Israel, and that leads to what the Lord did with him.

precepts.text: The Lord took away his sins, and exalted his horn for ever: he gave him a covenant of kings, and a throne of glory in Israel. The Lord forgave David; he loved David, and David messed up badly. A lot of times we are going to fall and do things that are not comely according to the scriptures. That does not mean you bunker down into a fetal position and say woe is me. You get yourself together, you repent, and you move forward. What did Christ say? Go, and sin no more. You pick up the pieces and keep moving. We are all going to make mistakes; it is how you handle the mistake.

precepts.why:
“The Lord took away his sins, and exalted his horn for ever: he gave him a covenant of kings, and a throne of glory in Israel.” The Lord did forgive David. He loved David, and David messed up.

David saw Bathsheba from the roof, took another man's wife, put Uriah in battle to be killed, and lost the child. That is as bad as it gets. But David repented, and the Lord took away his sins, exalted his horn, and gave him a covenant of kings and a throne of glory in Israel.

And that's another thing. A lot of times we are going to fall and do things that are not comely according to the scriptures. That don't mean you bunker down, go into a fetal position and say woe is me. You get yourself together, you repent, and you move forward. You don't go back. What did Christ say? Go, and sin no more.

You got to pick up the pieces and keep moving. We are all going to make mistakes. It is how you handle the mistake: it happened, so what are you going to do now, moving forward?

precepts.text: In all Israel there was none so much praised as Absalom for his beauty, without blemish from the sole of his foot to the crown of his head. Beauty became his identity, and behind it came ambition, rebellion against his father, civil war, and death hanging by that very hair. Whenever physical attraction is in the forefront, the Bible shows trouble behind it.
precepts.point: Y'all take chess and spades seriously, seeing moves ahead and counting books, but not marriage. She looks good, I have to marry her so I can have her.

note.label: Marriage Beyond Romance: From Eden to Modern Confusion

precepts.why:
“But in all Israel there was none to be so much praised as Absalom for his beauty: from the sole of his foot even to the crown of his head there was no blemish in him.” Beauty became part of Absalom's identity. It was synonymous with him: his hair, his physical perfection.

And what came behind that? Ambition and rebellion. You get a big head about yourself and you start to believe certain things. Absalom rose up against his father, it came to civil war, and he died hanging from that very hair, the same thing that was vanity to him.

That is the same lesson as David on the roof in 2 Samuel 11:2. David saw a woman “very beautiful to look upon”, he saw her, he inquired, and he took her, the same pattern as Shechem with Dinah. Out of one fleeting moment of attraction came adultery, the murder of Uriah, a national scandal, the death of the child, and chaos in David's house the rest of his days. The Lord forgave him, but he left him with drama for moving that way. Then Absalom, celebrated for his own beauty, came to pride and rebellion.

Whenever physical attraction becomes the forefront of anything, the Bible shows you that trouble comes behind it. Y'all take chess and spades seriously, seeing moves ahead and counting books, but not marriage: she look good, I got to marry her so I can have her. Attraction is the gateway to destruction if that is the only thing you are moving on.

precepts.text: Lust not after her beauty in thine heart, neither let her take thee with her eyelids. She gives you the look back, the sparks fly, and you have lost your mind.
precepts.point: Y'all take chess and spades seriously, seeing moves ahead and counting books, but not marriage. She looks good, I have to marry her so I can have her.

note.label: Marriage Beyond Romance: From Eden to Modern Confusion

precepts.why:
This is why the scripture says these things: “Lust not after her beauty in thine heart; neither let her take thee with her eyelids.” The scripture teaches you not to lust after her beauty, and it says where: in thy heart, in thy mind.

“neither let her take thee with her eyelids.” She gives you the look back. You make the eye contact, you feel the chemistry, the sparks fly, the tentacles of auras come out and they embrace, and you done lost your mind. I got to have her. Bring me that. That's what I want.

That is exactly what happened to David in 2 Samuel 11:2. He walked on the roof, saw a woman washing herself, “and the woman was very beautiful to look upon”, and he moved on what he saw. Shechem saw Dinah and took her, and it ended in violence and massacre. Samson went after the one who pleased him well, and it ended in betrayal and blindness. David saw Bathsheba's beauty, had to have her, and it ended in adultery and murder.

So Solomon's warning is the guard against the very thing David fell into: do not let the beauty get into your heart, and do not let the eyes take you. Attraction is not the foundation, and a man who moves on it alone gives up his strength.

precepts.text: A woman with the attire of an harlot, and subtil of heart. The physical again, meant to entice, and it works. Solomon knew how intoxicating it is; he said not one woman in a thousand.
precepts.point: Y'all take chess and spades seriously, seeing moves ahead and counting books, but not marriage. She looks good, I have to marry her so I can have her.

note.label: Marriage Beyond Romance: From Eden to Modern Confusion

precepts.why:
“And, behold, there met him a woman with the attire of an harlot, and subtil of heart.” There is the physical again: the attire of an harlot and subtil of heart. She is trying to entice, and you fall for it. It works.

Here Solomon warns about being captured by appearance. How does he know these things? He said not one out of a thousand of the women he dealt with. He knew, and he probably knew before the thousandth. It goes to show how intoxicating it can be. You get caught up.

That is the thread through David on the roof in 2 Samuel 11:2. Shechem saw Dinah and took her: violence and massacre. Samson, she pleased him well: betrayal and blindness. David saw Bathsheba's beauty and had to have her: adultery and murder. Absalom, celebrated for his own beauty: pride and rebellion. And the strange women, being beautiful, lead to ruin.

That is why the Bible rarely makes much of the beauty of wives. Rebecca is known for her character, her hospitality and her faith; Zipporah's beauty is never described; Elizabeth is called righteous, not beautiful. What is highlighted in our foremothers is righteousness, obedience, wisdom and faith. The Bible doesn't deny attraction; it just isn't the foundation.

precepts.text: Cursed is he that smiteth his neighbour secretly, and cursed is he that taketh reward to slay an innocent person.
precepts.point: David set this man up to get murdered, and Israel does this too, contrary to popular belief. This goes back to Deuteronomy 27: cursed is he that smiteth his neighbour secretly, because nobody knew what David was doing, and cursed is he that taketh reward to slay an innocent person. The reward was that woman; he slew an innocent man who had done nothing.

note.label: 2 Samuel 11: David, Bathsheba, and the Murder of Uriah

precepts.why:
“Cursed be he that smiteth his neighbour secretly. And all the people shall say, Amen. Cursed be he that taketh reward to slay an innocent person.”

David wrote a letter to Joab and sent it by the hand of Uriah himself: “Set ye Uriah in the forefront of the hottest battle, and retire ye from him, that he may be smitten, and die.” Joab assigned him to a place where he knew valiant men were, “and Uriah the Hittite died also.”

David set this man up to get murdered, and Israel does this too, contrary to popular belief. He smote his neighbour secretly, because nobody knew what David was doing. And he took reward to slay an innocent person: the reward was that woman, and he slew an innocent man who had done nothing. Both curses fall on this deed.

precepts.text: Joab was David's nephew and the go between in the matter of Bathsheba and the killing of Uriah; Joab knew David's dirt, which is why he often defied the king's orders.
precepts.point: Joab was an evil man with the spirit of murder; he could have brought Absalom back alive for his father to make amends, but he did what he wanted. Ten young men that bore Joab's armor compassed Absalom and smote him and slew him, for a beast will consort to his own like.

note.label: 2 Samuel 18: Deal Gently With the Young Man

precepts.why:
At “the time when kings go forth to battle”, David sent Joab out against the children of Ammon, “But David tarried still at Jerusalem.” From the roof he saw Bath-sheba, sent and took her, and when she was with child, “David sent to Joab, saying, Send me Uriah the Hittite. And Joab sent Uriah to David.”

Joab was David’s nephew and the go between in the matter of Bathsheba and the killing of Uriah. Joab knew David’s dirt, which is why he often defied the king’s orders.

And here he defied them. The man who saw Absalom hanged in an oak would not touch him for a thousand shekels, “for in our hearing the king charged thee and Abishai and Ittai, saying, Beware that none touch the young man Absalom.” Joab said, “I may not tarry thus with thee”, took three darts, “and thrust them through the heart of Absalom, while he was yet alive in the midst of the oak.”

Joab was an evil man with the spirit of murder. He could have brought Absalom back alive for his father to make amends, but he did what he wanted. Ten young men that bare Joab’s armour compassed about and smote Absalom and slew him, for a beast will consort to his own like.

They called it the expiration, meaning the end, not January 1st. “For at the return of the year”: the return of the year is the same thing as the expiration of the year; once the year ends a new year starts. “The king of Syria will come up against thee”: in ancient biblical times all the kings took heed to this; the majority of the wars were fought at the expiration of the year, the springtime.
“And it came to pass at the return of the year”: springtime. “That Ben–hadad numbered the Syrians, and went up to Aphek, to fight against Israel.”

“And when the year was expired”: springtime, not January 1st. “King Nebuchadnezzar sent, and brought him to Babylon”. Zedekiah did evil, “but he stiffened his neck, and hardened his heart from turning unto the Lord God of Israel.” “But they mocked the messengers of God, and despised his words, and misused his prophets, until the wrath of the Lord arose against his people, till there was no remedy.” He brought upon them the king of the Chaldees, and all the vessels and treasures were brought to Babylon. When did this happen? Springtime.

When King David’s men went to war he was supposed to go with them; that was the first mistake he made. “There shall not any man be able to stand before thee all the days of thy life”: verse 4 is what Amalek, the so-called fake Jewish gutter rat in the land of Israel, is trying to accomplish, but he will not accomplish it. In the book of Joshua, Joshua was always involved in the wars of the Lord; he was leading the charge, the one Moses put in charge of the people. It was the king’s job to go to war with his soldiers.

Another example, King Saul. “And the Spirit of God came upon Saul when he heard those tidings, and his anger was kindled greatly”: for our brothers and sisters coming out of the Christian church who are still confused. Anger is a damn attribute of the Lord; that’s why the Bible says he’s a man of war, not this damn Christian spirit you got with your head stuck up the white man’s ass. Some of that anger got to get on you brothers in Israel United in Christ so you can step up your teaching at camp or in the classroom when you see the conditions of our people; some of you are too damn comfortable letting Christianity seep in. “And slew the Ammonites until the heat of the day”: the heat of the day is high noon. The Most High is a genius: what is Ammon’s flag, what do they call Japan? The Rising Sun. When his soldiers went to war, the king went with them.

David’s first mistake was idleness. “Send him to labour, that he be not idle; for idleness teacheth much evil.” Brothers and sisters, you have some downtime, you just scrolling, and boop, an image pops up on Instagram and you entertain it. Idle time is the playground of the devil. If you had been keeping yourself busy, watching the class, talking to a brother or sister, that would not have happened. Whenever we fall into sin it’s because of idle time.

“For the corruptible body presseth down the soul”: our bodies are corruptible because they are prone to sin. The soul is where the seed of the laws of God should be; the body wants to do evil but the soul wants to do good. “And the earthy tabernacle”: that fleshly body. “Weigheth down the mind that museth upon many things”: why does the mind muse upon many things? Because you have idle time; that’s where your mind starts to wander.

“For from within, out of the heart of men, proceed evil thoughts”: the heart of men meaning the mind; that’s where thoughts come from. “Adulteries, fornications”: notice he didn’t put eating pork or unclean food first, because the majority of us got that in check. What’s plaguing us is adultery and fornication. “Lasciviousness”: foot fetishes and all kinds of fetishes, pedophilia, role play, the father and son role play porn. What the hell is going on? I didn’t hear too much about bestiality, but brothers are fighting that spirit: you see a damn pitbull and think the pitbull is attractive? The hell is this. “An evil eye”.

David should have had more constraint over his eyes, which is his body part. “I made a covenant with mine eyes; why then should I think upon a maid?” “For what portion of God is there from above? and what inheritance of the Almighty from on high?”

His second mistake was not constraining his eyes. “Remember that a wicked eye is an evil thing: and what is created more wicked than an eye?” “Therefore it weepeth upon every occasion”: that’s why we got to get our eye in control. What we see through our eyes becomes thoughts, and eventually our thoughts become actions; that’s what happened with King David.

“But I say unto you, That whosoever looketh on a woman to lust after her hath committed adultery with her already in his heart”: same thing with pornography; you’re looking on a woman and lusting after her. David saw Bathsheba taking a shower, looked one second too long, and already imagined what he wanted to do with her before he called her up to his chambers. “And if thy right eye offend thee, pluck it out, and cast it from thee”: that’s why we have checks, brothers who call and check up on you; we even put passwords on brothers’ phones and computers that only the next brother would know. And one brother went to the store, purchased another laptop just to watch porn, and returned the laptop. Can’t make this up. Whatever barrier we put around brothers, they’ll find a way, because we are wise to do evil. “For it is profitable for thee that one of thy members should perish, and not that thy whole body should be cast into hell”: throw the phone away, throw the computer away, throw the magazine away; not the whole body, meaning your soul.

“For the commandment is a lamp; and the law is light”: all we can give you is the commandments; that’s the only light that can illuminate your dark path on porn, adultery and fornication. “Neither let her take thee with her eyelids”: for her to take you with her eyelids you have to be looking at her eyelids, so everything starts with the eye. “For by means of a whorish woman a man is brought to a piece of bread: and the adulteress will hunt for the precious life”: brothers, you are that precious life. Each of us is a literal member of Christ; he took a part of himself and made you, so when you give yourself to a harlot you’re cursing Christ and spitting in his face. “Can a man take fire in his bosom, and his clothes not be burned?” You will get burned; eventually you’ll want to enact the real thing. And if you’re one of those strong brothers who can watch porn and not do it physically, you’re still damning your soul; a chronic porn watcher is not going to inherit the kingdom of God. But Christ is giving you that grace under the New Covenant to overcome; if you’re still breathing to watch this class, that’s the grace to overcome, so you don’t get turned into a piece of bread.

The third mistake was the abuse of power. “Learn, ye that be judges of the ends of the earth”: the kings are the judges; King David was supposed to bring forth righteous judgment. “For power is given you of the Lord”: the Most High gave King David this authority. “Because, being ministers of his kingdom, ye have not judged aright, nor kept the law”: that’s when he fell into adultery and broke the law. The Most High gave him the authority and he abused it, because Bathsheba, the messengers and the guards were not going to say no, and David knew that.

“That he shall write him a copy of this law in a book”: that’s the Torah. “And he shall read therein all the days of his life”: that’s the job of the king. “That his heart be not lifted up above his brethren”: your mind gets lifted up above your brothers until you start to usurp and abuse the authority you have over people.

They may add sin to sin. “Woe to the rebellious children, saith the Lord, that take counsel, but not of me; and that cover with a covering, but not of my spirit, that they may add sin to sin”: that’s exactly what we see going on with King David, adding sin to sin at different levels.

This is a beautiful chapter. “Blessed is he whose transgression is forgiven, whose sin is covered.” “When I kept silence, my bones waxed old through my roaring all the day long.” “I acknowledged my sin unto thee”: King David eventually got to that point after he got checked by the prophet. “I said, I will confess my transgressions unto the Lord; and thou forgavest the iniquity of my sin.” When you confess your transgression to the Lord and you stop it, stop the fornication, the adultery, the pornography, that’s when the Most High forgives you. “For this shall every one that is godly pray unto thee in a time when thou mayest be found”.

“I made haste, and delayed not to keep thy commandments.” This is important because tomorrow is not promised. Some of us walk around like the Most High owes us a tomorrow. The Most High don’t owe us a damn thing, not a second later, not a good night or a good morning. You act like you got all the time in the world to repent, a notorious liar, hater, pornographer, adulterer, fornicator, on and on like a wheelbarrow that keeps spinning. He don’t owe you; you owe him. King David said he made haste to repent.

You want to know why we’re not prospering as a people and individually? Because we are covering our sins; we have not confessed or forsaken them. “But whoso confesseth and forsaketh them shall have mercy”: forsaketh meaning to stop doing it, so next week or next month you’re not praying to the Lord to forgive you for that same sin.
“Return unto the Lord, and forsake thy sins”: return unto the Lord, Israel, and stop doing it. “Make thy prayer before his face, and offend less”: stop being that repetitive, notorious sinner.

This is the point we all have to reach. “I will set no wicked thing before mine eyes”. After the judgment the Most High brought on King David, do you think he went back on his balcony staring at the sisters taking a shower? Hell to the no. He made haste, repented, went through his judgment, and continued on with the mission; you never read about him falling back into that. Set no pornography before your eyes. “I hate the work of them that turn aside; it shall not cleave to me”: we got to get to the point where we hate and despise sin; you hate porn, you hate watching women in spandex and tight jeans, whatever your device is. “I will not know a wicked person.”

“And one that feared God, and eschewed evil.” The first step is to fear God, because once you fear God you’re going to eschew evil, meaning hate evil; those two go hand in hand. Same thing King David said in Psalms 101.

“Set a mark upon the foreheads of the men that sigh and that cry for all the abominations that be done in the midst thereof”: you’re not going to sigh and cry, brothers and sisters, if you don’t hate evil. That mark is being sealed with the laws of God in your mind. “And to the others he said in mine hearing”: the others who are watching porn and won’t stop committing adultery and fornication. In mine hearing: the Most High wants to hear you scream, hear the pain of death, hear you holler. “Slay utterly old and young, both maids, and little children, and women”: the old man can get it, the young man can get it, and your little nasty children can get it, because you got kids on these sites meeting boys and girls on FaceTime; we had situations like that. And the woman ain’t absolved. “And begin at my sanctuary”: judgment must first begin at the house of Israel before the Most High deals with the other nations. He’s going to start with us first.

“Love not the world, neither the things that are in the world.” Some of us love the things of the world; that’s how you get pulled into these sins. “If any man love the world, the love of the Father is not in him”: you love pornography, fornication, adultery, the love of the Father is not in you. “The lust of the flesh, and the lust of the eyes”: that’s why Job said make a covenant with your eyes. We get enticed by what we see and also by what we hear. A brother on a blitz in a hotel heard somebody next door having sex, and instead of putting on his headphones and listening to class, he went on porn. Another brother at a construction site was enticed by his co-workers’ talk, an old demon he was battling; he called crying, and we had another brother meet him and put a block on his computer. “And the pride of life”: then you fall into LGBTQ pride, gay pride; putting your own emotions and instant gratification before the laws of God. The lust of the eyes is one of the three main sources of temptation from the world; our desires originate from what we see, and those thoughts become actions.

Now some ways to resist. “Wherewithal shall a young man cleanse his way?” All of us are young men, especially young in this truth. “By taking heed thereto according to thy word”: we all have ears, but are you listening? When you take heed, whatever you hear you enact. When Christ says cast off your member, you’re supposed to put a block on the sites you entertain, get rid of that laptop or phone, go back to a BlackBerry or flip phone. Like Bishop always says, are you studying, praying and applying? Are you reading Isaiah and Ezekiel or the book of Janet Jack and Heather Hunter? “With my whole heart have I sought thee: O let me not wander from thy commandments.”

“Flee also youthful lusts”: we’ve been watching porn since our early teenage years, some brothers since 9 or 10 years old; when you’re an adolescent burning, that’s youthful lust. “But follow righteousness”: by taking heed to the commandments of God, which is more than listening; it’s the application of God’s laws. “With them that call on the Lord out of a pure heart.”

“And have no fellowship with the unfruitful works of darkness”: not some fellowship, not a little pocket of sin left open. Those works can come by family, friends, your job, the social media avenues. “But rather reprove them”: some of you got to cut off your friends who still bring up worldly conversation, cut off family members who are wicked as hell, and limit the time you talk to co-workers whose conversation leads you to porn, fornication and adultery. This scripture doesn’t change person to person; there’s no magical Shazam Marvel superhero scripture. The Most High wants you to fight; every moment you have the breath of life, that’s the grace under Christ to get it right. How long you going to be fighting with youthful lust, that chronic masturbator, chronic foot fetish, chronic crossdresser? We got to get it together.

Some of that unfruitful work of darkness is social media. You scroll and a naked woman or a woman in lingerie or a bikini pops up on your feed; it’s up to you to show constraint and not click and entertain it, because then you’re break dancing with the devil in his playground, and he got more moves than you. “Be not deceived”: you’re deceiving yourself saying you can handle it, just a little bit. You enter one doorway of woman and woman porn and come out another doorway of two men, bestiality or pedophilia. “Evil communications corrupt good manners”: the good manners of God’s laws, statutes and commandments that are supposed to resonate in our soul. Brothers over the camps: if those battling porn are serious, they will let you put a block on their phone or laptop. There should be a check system in all the congregations so we can hold each other accountable; that’s charity, loving your neighbour as yourself.

Another avenue: “Nevertheless, to avoid fornication, let every man have his own wife”. We don’t understand how a brother could be eight or ten years in the truth and not married. Everybody think they Paul; you ain’t Paul. You’re doing something, hitting something, out with lot lizards and prostitutes, and the brothers fighting the homosexuality spirit, same thing. Check that sin first and then get married. “And let every woman have her own husband”: your own, one.

points: And it came to pass in an eveningtide, that David arose from off his bed, and walked upon the roof of the king's house: and from the roof he saw a woman washing herself; and the woman was very beautiful to look upon.
And David sent and enquired after the woman. And one said, Is not this Bathsheba, the daughter of Eliam, the wife of Uriah the Hittite?
And David sent messengers, and took her; and she came in unto him, and he lay with her; for she was purified from her uncleanness: and she returned unto her house.

And he wrote in the letter, saying, Set ye Uriah in the forefront of the hottest battle, and retire ye from him, that he may be smitten, and die. Somebody explain what just happened. From the floor: King David just plotted against Uriah, for Bathsheba, to set him up to be killed in the battle.

But hold on a second. Did King Saul not try to do that to him? Same thing. Remember I made a statement earlier that you may not be tempted by that bitterness now. Just wait. So right now King David is no longer on the run. He is back in his kingship, back in his palace, back in his rightful place. And that same spirit tempted him. And his was through coveting his neighbour's house. So through that covetousness it compounded with hatred and bitterness.

So a lot of the time we are like, oh no, I am not dealing with that. Do you think David thought, when he was running from King Saul, that he would have to be dealing with the same thing? Everyone always thinks all Bishop's classes are about everybody else. All the deacon's classes are about everybody else. Well, which one is about you? Just give it time.

David arose from off his bed, walked upon the roof of the king's house, and from the roof he saw a woman washing herself; and the woman was very beautiful to look upon. He saw her and sent to inquire after the woman: I have power, let me send some people over there.

You see how Satan can deceive you. Satan put that lust in him to where he just did not care, and he went the extra mile: later in the story he put Uriah in the front of the battle and got him killed, then took the wife. What he saw became desire, desire became action, he tried to cover it up, and the consequences came: the child died.

And one said, Is not this Bathsheba, the daughter of Eliam, the wife of Uriah the Hittite? Somebody with a spiritual mind made it clear: this is somebody's wife. And David sent messengers, and took her anyway. Wisdom and understanding were right there, and he ignored them.

And she came in unto him, and he lay with her. She was not right either: she did not resist, she was not opposed; she thought she came up. And the woman conceived, and sent and told David, and said, I am with child.

David walked on the roof and saw a woman washing herself, and she was very beautiful to look upon. He saw, inquired, and took, the same pattern as Shechem. Out of one fleeting moment of attraction came adultery, the murder of Uriah, a national scandal, the death of the child, and chaos in David's house for the rest of his days, though the Lord forgave him.
Y'all take chess and spades seriously, seeing moves ahead and counting books, but not marriage. She looks good, I have to marry her so I can have her.

note.label: Marriage Beyond Romance: From Eden to Modern Confusion

points: After the year was expired, at the time when kings go forth to battle, David sent Joab and all Israel to destroy the children of Ammon and besiege Rabbah, but David tarried still at Jerusalem. In the evening he walked upon the roof, saw a woman washing herself who was very beautiful, inquired and learned she was Bathsheba the wife of Uriah the Hittite, sent and took her, and lay with her; and she conceived and told David, I am with child.

Masons and people in these fraternities always run here to justify wrongdoing, saying David slept with Bathsheba and the Most High still forgave him. But you are not King David; David was a man like the rest of us, and he messed up, and this is the mess up. About ninety percent of them go right back to David and Bathsheba every time they want to justify some wrongdoing.

note.label: 2 Samuel 11: David, Bathsheba, and the Murder of Uriah

points: David's plan, which nobody was privy to, was that if Uriah went down and slept with his wife, they could say the child was his. A lot of us do that today: many people raise children that are not theirs, and just because David did it does not make it right.

note.label: 2 Samuel 11: David, Bathsheba, and the Murder of Uriah

points: David sent to Joab to send him Uriah. When Uriah came, David asked how Joab and the people did and how the war prospered, then told him to go down to his house and wash his feet, sending a mess of meat after him. But Uriah slept at the door of the king's house with the servants of his lord and went not down to his house. When David heard it, he asked Uriah why he came not from his journey and went not down.

note.label: 2 Samuel 11: David, Bathsheba, and the Murder of Uriah

points: Uriah told David that the ark and Israel and Judah abode in tents, and Joab and the servants of his lord were encamped in the open fields; so how could he go into his house to eat, drink, and lie with his wife? As David lived, he would not do this thing. David kept him another day and made him drunk, but that evening Uriah still went out to lie on his bed with the servants of his lord and went not down to his house.

note.label: 2 Samuel 11: David, Bathsheba, and the Murder of Uriah

points: Uriah had a sense of loyalty that was probably killing David all the more, because David could not deceive this man into laying with his wife. Even drunk, when a man might just go home to sleep it off, Uriah still slept at David's house and would not go down.

note.label: 2 Samuel 11: David, Bathsheba, and the Murder of Uriah

points: In the morning David wrote a letter to Joab and sent it by the hand of Uriah, ordering that Uriah be set in the forefront of the hottest battle and then abandoned, that he might be smitten and die. Joab assigned Uriah to a place where he knew valiant men were, and when the men of the city fought, some of David's servants fell, and Uriah the Hittite died also.

note.label: 2 Samuel 11: David, Bathsheba, and the Murder of Uriah

points: Other men of Israel died too, not just Uriah, so with David's sin other men died as well. Joab knew what the king really wanted, so he made sure to name Uriah as dead. David's reply was that it is what it is, the mission was accomplished, you win some and lose some; being content with murder is a wicked thing to do.

note.label: 2 Samuel 11: David, Bathsheba, and the Murder of Uriah

points: Joab sent and told David all concerning the war, charging the messenger that if the king's wrath arose over drawing so nigh the city, he should then say that Uriah the Hittite was dead also. When the messenger delivered it, David told him to say to Joab, Let not this thing displease thee, for the sword devoureth one as well as another; make the battle stronger and overthrow the city.

note.label: 2 Samuel 11: David, Bathsheba, and the Murder of Uriah

points: When the wife of Uriah heard her husband was dead, she mourned for him, and when the mourning was past, David sent and fetched her to his house and she became his wife and bare him a son. But the thing that David had done displeased the Most High.

It displeased the Most High because it was murder; he set the man up to be murdered on a battlefield, which was not a righteous thing. Bathsheba was not innocent either; she was complicit. When David called for her she went, she did not refuse because she was married, and it was consensual, not rape. She knew she was pregnant, so this was deceitful on both sides.

note.label: 2 Samuel 11: David, Bathsheba, and the Murder of Uriah

points: I love reading about our forefather King David. As great as he was, called a friend of God, he had flaws, and many of his flaws are our flaws. Like we read in James, there are different steps into that sin; ask yourself what was the root cause. In chapter 10 David just came from a war; chapter 11 is where the sin starts.

“After the year was expired”: write this down so you’ll never be confounded by a Christian apologist. January 1 is not the new year according to the Bible; the year starts in the springtime, depending on when the new moon comes in. Expired means to end. “At the time when kings go forth to battle”: in the ancient Eastern world kings went forth to battle in the springtime, with more provisions and crops for the soldiers and good weather. The Department of Defense itself writes that daylight saving time was once known as war time, first official in America on March 19th 1918 under the Standard Time Act, to save energy during World War One. Spring forward: Esau got that from the Bible.

“But David tarried still at Jerusalem”: one word, idleness. Write down the consequences of David’s idleness. He was supposed to go to war and he did not, so he had idle time on his hands. As Saturday’s class said, there are so many things in IUIC to keep you busy: fold flyers, visit a brother, go over scriptures, classes all day every day. Idleness builds a mental and spiritual void; David’s idling gave temptation space to grow unchecked, a snowball of sin that led to his adultery and eventually a plot to put Uriah to death. That was his first mistake.

“In an eveningtide, that David arose from off his bed, and walked upon the roof of the king’s house”: remember it’s springtime and the weather’s nice; nobody takes a bath outside in the winter. “And the woman was very beautiful to look upon”: the eyes look, and the more time goes by, the mind starts to think thoughts. Same thing with pornography and these Instagram posts: one second, two seconds, five seconds, and next thing you know you’re clicking, because you done concocted a whole scene in your mind with yourself and that woman, and now you want to see it played out. David should have had more constraint over his eyes; he looked one second too long and imagined a whole scene. That was his second mistake.

“And David sent and enquired after the woman”: they told him she was married, the wife of Uriah the Hittite. “And David sent messengers, and took her”: he still sent, because the lust was already inflamed; he’s like, I have to have this woman. That was his third mistake, the abuse of power. Who’s going to tell the king no? She ain’t going to tell him no, and the messengers who fetched Bathsheba knew she wasn’t going up there to talk about the Ammonites he slew in chapter 10, or to make unleavened bread or sew garments; he already had servants and committees for that. There was no reason to summon her except adultery. The security guards outside his bedchamber heard what was going on and ain’t nobody knocked on the door, because they knew David would put their ass to death.

Now you have idleness, no constraint of the eyes, abuse of power, and now deception and cover-up; write that down. A brother added that each step plays out what James said: first you conceive it in your mind, you saw it, you lusted after it, then you put your hands to it, and in that abuse of power David, as spiritual as he was, completely lost the spirit through his lust.

Uriah came back from the war and slept at the door of the king’s house with all the servants; he was fervent to be close to the king and to fight for his people. This was a just man. “The ark, and Israel, and Judah, abide in tents”: “shall I then go into mine house, to eat and to drink, and to lie with my wife?” This is charity, true love; he’s putting the mission before his spouse. I’ll say it again, some people might get hurt: the mission is more important than our spouses, the mission of resurrecting the 12 tribes of Israel and bringing forth Christ’s kingdom.
Why was David trying to get this man to go to his wife? This is the start of the deception: David wanted Uriah to sleep with his wife so that when the baby came Uriah would think it was his.

“And he made him drunk”: are we supposed to make people drunk? When you get drunk, that’s a sin. You can drink, but there’s a limit; the scripture says to be sober minded. David has been turned into a piece of bread; he’s superbly desperate at this time.

“Set ye Uriah in the forefront of the hottest battle, and retire ye from him, that he may be smitten, and die.” That’s some cold-blooded stuff right there. That’s the depths of adultery, of madness, of being turned into a piece of bread. Look at all the steps: the idleness which started it all, not controlling his eyes, laying with the sister, covering it up by getting the husband to sleep with her, then getting him drunk, and then the forefront of the hottest battle. The end result: death.
